nameStory: The 'arumleaf' part of this plant's name comes from its distinctive leaves that resemble those of wild arum plants, with their broad, arrow-like shape. 'Arrowhead' refers to the classic pointed leaf shape that looks just like the tip of an arrow or spear. The alternative name 'duck potato' hints at its starchy, edible tubers that waterfowl love to dig up and munch on.
description: Arumleaf arrowhead is an aquatic perennial plant that grows in shallow water and wet areas throughout New England. It produces distinctive arrow-shaped leaves that emerge from the water on long stems, along with delicate white flowers held above the water surface on separate stalks. The plant typically reaches 1-3 feet tall and spreads by underground tubers. Like other arrowheads, it's an important food source for waterfowl and a beautiful addition to wetland communities.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Classic arrow-shaped leaves with a broad base and pointed tip, feeling smooth and somewhat waxy to the touch. The leaf blade is typically wider than it is long, giving it a distinctly triangular appearance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: White flowers with three rounded petals arranged in whorls along an upright stalk. Each flower is about an inch across and has a papery texture, with bright yellow centers that attract pollinators.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Emerges from shallow water or muddy shorelines with leaves and flower stalks rising separately from the base. Forms colonies through underground tubers that feel firm and potato-like when dug up.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces dense, round clusters of small, flattened seeds that feel rough and have distinctive beaked tips. The seed heads turn brown and papery as they mature in late summer.

habitat: Found in shallow ponds, lake margins, slow streams, and marshy areas throughout New England. Prefers muddy or sandy bottoms in water that's 6 inches to 2 feet deep, often growing alongside cattails, pickerelweed, and other aquatic plants. Thrives in both sunny and partially shaded wetlands from sea level to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: New arrow-shaped leaves begin emerging from the water as temperatures warm, unfurling from tight spirals. Early leaves may be more rounded before developing their characteristic pointed shape.
seasonality.summer: White flowers bloom from June through August, standing tall above the water on separate stalks. This is the best time for identification when both distinctive leaves and flowers are present.
seasonality.fall: Seed heads mature and turn brown while leaves begin to yellow and die back. Underground tubers are at their largest and most nutritious for wildlife.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely above ground, leaving only dormant tubers buried in the mud. Look for dried seed stalks poking through ice or lying along shorelines.

funFact: Native Americans and early settlers harvested arrowhead tubers as 'duck potatoes' - they taste remarkably similar to regular potatoes when cooked and were so valued that some tribes established specific gathering territories around prime arrowhead marshes!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with broadleaf arrowhead, which has longer, narrower leaves and grows much larger overall. Remember: arumleaf arrowhead has leaves that are wider than they are long, like a broad triangle, while broadleaf arrowhead's leaves are longer than wide, like a narrow spearpoint.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'wapato' comes from the Chinook word for these plants and their edible tubers, reflecting their importance to indigenous peoples across North America. Don't confuse this aquatic plant with the unrelated houseplant called 'arrowhead vine' - they just happen to share a similar leaf shape.
compareHints: Among New England's arrowheads, arumleaf arrowhead is distinguished by its relatively broad, triangular leaves that are wider than they are long. Broadleaf arrowhead has much longer, narrower arrow-shaped leaves, while grass-leaved arrowhead has thin, strap-like leaves with no arrow shape at all. The compact, broad leaf shape of arumleaf arrowhead makes it quite distinctive once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Broadleaf arrowhead stands out from its relatives by having the widest, most pronounced arrow-shaped leaves in the genus - while grass-leaved arrowhead has narrow, strap-like leaves and slender arrowhead has thin, linear foliage.
Among New England's arrowheads, grass-leaved arrowhead is instantly recognizable by its narrow, grass-like leaves – all other species have distinctly arrow-shaped or oval leaves.
While broadleaf arrowhead has classic arrow-shaped leaves and grass-leaved arrowhead has broader, ribbon-like foliage, slender arrowhead's leaves are so narrow they look like green needles.
Compared to the common broadleaf arrowhead, Midwestern arrowhead has more narrow, elongated leaf lobes and distinctly shorter beaks on its fruits.
Unlike broadleaf arrowhead with its iconic three-pointed arrow leaves, sessile-fruited arrowhead has narrow ovals.
Among the arrowhead family, Engelmann's stands out for its extremely narrow leaf lobes and strict preference for acidic water.
Among New England's arrowheads, Spongy Arrowhead is distinguished by its uniquely soft, air-filled leaf stalks - a feature no other local Sagittaria species shares.
Among New England arrowheads, delta arrowhead has broader, more triangular leaves than the common broadleaf arrowhead, and much wider leaves than the grass-like narrow-leaved arrowhead.
Among New England's arrowheads, this species stands out for having the thinnest, most grass-like leaves - much narrower even than grass-leaved arrowhead.

Among New England arrowheads, hooded arrowhead is unique for its curved sepals that hood over the flower petals, while broadleaf arrowhead has flat, open flowers and grass-leaved arrowhead has narrow, grass-like leaves rather than the broad arrow shape.
